title: How Rising Material Costs Widen Scope Gaps on Lump Sum Bids
summary: Input prices rose at a 12.6% annualized rate in early 2026. Every unpriced scope gap hits harder. Here's how GCs protect margin.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Nonresidential construction input prices rose at a 12.6% annualized rate in early 2026, based on the producer price index readings for construction inputs and driven largely by tariff-related material cost increases. That is a short-period rate projected out to a year, not a confirmed year-over-year increase.
- On a lump sum contract, every unpriced scope item is now more expensive than it was 12 months ago. The gap between what you priced and what it costs to build is wider.
- Scope gaps have always cost money. In 2026, they cost more money, faster.
- The GCs protecting margin are doing two things: writing tighter scope packages before bid day, and reviewing contracts for risk clauses before they sign.
- Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) and[Risk Review](https://provision.com/risk-review) tools are built specifically for that pre-bid and pre-signing workflow.


## The Problem With Lump Sum Bids When Input Costs Spike


A lump sum contract is a fixed-price bet. You price the work, the owner signs, and anything that costs more than you planned comes out of your margin. That is the deal.


When material costs are stable, that bet is manageable. When input prices climb at a 12.6% annualized rate, the bet gets harder to win.


The issue is not the materials you priced. Those are in your number. The issue is the materials you did not price because a scope item was unclear, omitted from a subcontractor's bid, or buried in a specification section nobody flagged.


That is what a scope gap is: work that is reasonably part of the project but has no line item in your estimate. At 2024 input prices, a missed roof cover board might cost you $400,000. At 2026 prices, that same gap hits harder before you even start the conversation about who is responsible.


## What 12.6% Actually Means for a Lump Sum Bid


A 12.6% annualized increase in nonresidential construction input costs is not evenly distributed. Some material categories are rising faster. Some trades are absorbing more of the cost than others. But across the board, the same scope item that was adequately priced in 2024 may now be underpriced by a meaningful margin.


Consider a few scenarios:


- A structural steel package with a $1.2M estimate carries roughly $150,000 more risk per year at current input cost trends, before you account for scope ambiguity.
- A mechanical scope that relied on a subcontractor's allowance for generator field conditioning now has less buffer. That category of cost has historically been a source of significant disputes on ICI projects. Providers expect to be made whole on conditioning costs that were not explicitly scoped.
- An envelope package where flashings, caulking, and cover board were not explicitly assigned to any trade is now a gap worth more than it was at award.


The math is simple: a fixed-price contract locks your revenue. Rising input costs raise the floor on what it actually costs to build. Every unpriced item widens the gap between those two numbers.


## Scope Gaps Are Not Random. They Are Caused.


This is the central argument in[The Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) , which draws on research with more than 200 general contractors across North America. Scope gaps are produced by a small set of consistent habits, most of them baked into how pre-construction teams work under time pressure.


The most common anti-pattern is also the most dangerous: writing scope packages from boilerplate rather than from the actual drawings and specifications for the project in front of you. When material costs are rising and "as-built" costs differ from prior projects, a boilerplate scope is a liability.


A Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC put it this way: "If you miss anything, they'll bill it." That was true before tariffs. It is more true now.


### The Anti-Patterns That Compound in a High-Cost Environment


Several habits that were marginal risks in a stable cost environment become significant exposures when input prices are elevated:


- **"As per plans and specs."** This is the most-cited anti-pattern among experienced estimators. It sounds thorough. It is not. It leaves responsibility undefined, and when a sub says "that is not in my number," you have no specific document reference to push back with.
- **Copy-paste from the previous similar job.** Two healthcare projects are never identical. Two office towers in the same city may have different spec sections for the same trade. Copying scope from a prior job means pricing the wrong project.
- **Junior estimators stuffing previous scopes verbatim.** The scope sheet from a 2022 project does not account for 2026 input costs, 2026 spec revisions, or the specific conditions on this site.
- **The five-minutes-before-bid review.** A scope review done at 3:00 PM on bid day is not a review. It is a signature.
- **Trusting subs on a gentleman's agreement.** An Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC noted that subcontractors have shifted. "We have less subs who just kind of a gentleman's agreement. They've become more quick to clarify that we're not including that one piece of scope." Informal coverage assumptions now carry formal cost consequences.


## Three Real Scope Gaps and What They Cost at Today's Prices


These examples come from operator interviews conducted for[The Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) . They illustrate the kind of gaps that exist on most large commercial projects, and why they are more expensive to absorb in 2026 than they were two years ago.


### The $400K Roof Cover Board


On a $50M commercial project, a roof cover board was not explicitly assigned in the envelope scope. No trade claimed it. The GC absorbed the cost and recovered it only through a relational concession from the subcontractor, not through contract language.


At 2026 input prices, the same gap costs more to close, and the relational concession is harder to extract. Subcontractors watching their own margins are not volunteering to absorb costs that were not in their bid.


### The $300K Lead-Lined Glass


On a hospital imaging suite, lead-lined glass was omitted from the scope package. The spec called for it. The GC absorbed the cost under "readily inferable" language in the contract.


This is the kind of gap that experienced estimators know to look for in healthcare specs. But on a project with 2,000 pages of documentation, finding it under time pressure requires deliberate process, not luck.


### The $45K Stone-Depth Mismatch


On a single slab, civil, structural, and architectural drawings showed different stone depths. The conflict was not caught before bid day. The discrepancy cost $45,000 to resolve in the field.


At current labor and material rates, that same drawing conflict costs more to resolve today than it would have in 2024.


## Lump Sum Contracts Put the Risk Entirely on the GC


This is not a novel observation, but it bears repeating in the current cost environment. Under a lump sum contract, the owner's exposure is capped. Yours is not.


Contract language around "readily inferable" scope, "work reasonably inferable from the contract documents," and similar phrases is designed to broaden GC responsibility without explicitly pricing it. When input costs are high, that language is more expensive than it looks.


A Senior PM at a Canadian ICI GC framed it plainly: "Our construction management clients expect us to find the scope gaps in the design too now. They expect us to be designers and engineers."


That expectation is encoded in the contract. And the cost of meeting it is rising.


For a deeper look at how contract language creates scope exposure, the chapter on[subcontract language and scope](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/subcontract-language-scope) in The Scope Gap Playbook is worth reading before your next bid.


## What the Best Pre-Construction Teams Do Differently


The GCs with the best margins in a high-cost environment are not doing something exotic. They are doing the basics more consistently than their competitors. The Scope Gap Playbook identifies eight habits that separate high-margin pre-construction teams from the rest. Three of them matter most when input costs are volatile.


### Habit 1: Drawings First, Not Boilerplate First


Start every scope package from the actual drawings and specifications for this project. Use templates as a starting point, not as the answer. A template is a floor. The project documents are the ceiling.


This sounds obvious. It is not universal. Under time pressure, teams reach for the last similar job. That habit is affordable when costs are stable. It is expensive when they are not.


### Habit 2: Specific Document References


Every scope line should cite the section, page, and detail number that governs it. "As per plans and specs" is not a reference. It is a gap in disguise.


When a sub disputes coverage, a specific document reference gives you a position. A generic reference gives you an argument.


### Habit 3: The Pre-Issue Scope Review Checkpoint


Before the scope package goes to subs, one person reviews it against the full project document set. Not the drawings only. Not the specs only. Both, together, including addenda.


The goal is to catch conflicts, missing trade assignments, and specification callouts that did not make it into the scope. Done right, this review takes time. Done with the right tools, it takes less time than you expect.

## The Trade-Specific Gaps Most Likely to Widen in 2026


Not every scope gap carries the same risk in a high-cost environment. Some trade categories have more exposure right now because their input costs are rising faster, or because the specification complexity makes gaps more likely. For detailed trade-by-trade examples, the[trade-specific scope gaps chapter](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) of the playbook covers the most common omissions by trade.


Trade High-Risk Scope Gap Category Why It Matters More in 2026


Structural Steel Embeds, anchor bolts, hoisting and rigging Steel and fastener prices sensitive to tariff-driven input cost increases


MEP Generator field conditioning, motor starters, fire-rated louvres Historically disputed; costs harder to absorb at elevated base prices


Envelope Roof cover board, masonry-storefront flashings, fire-stopping Often unassigned between trades; gap cost rises with material prices


Concrete Grouting base plates, concrete pumping, slab assembly conflicts Drawing conflicts between structural and architectural become more costly


Specialty Lead-lined glass, curtainwall mock-ups, mass-timber material protection Specification-heavy items easy to miss in a 2,000-page document set


## What You Can Do Before the Next Bid Closes


You cannot control input costs. You can control scope coverage. These are the actions that move the needle before bid day:


1. **Start from drawings, not boilerplate.** Every bid. No exceptions.
2. **Assign every trade explicitly.** If it appears in the specifications, it needs a home in the scope package.
3. **Reference specific document sections.** Replace "as per plans and specs" with section numbers, detail callouts, and page references.
4. **Run a pre-issue scope review.** One person checks the package against the full document set before it goes to subs.
5. **Flag contract risk clauses before you sign.** Identify every clause that expands GC responsibility under "readily inferable" or similar language.
6. **Use tools built for construction documents.** Generic AI does not read drawings or cross-reference spec sections.[Purpose-built tools for general contractors](https://provision.com/general-contractors) do.


A Senior PM on an owner's rep team put the ROI calculation simply: "If we could catch three scope gaps or three missed items on every scope of work, then this thing pays for itself." At 2026 input prices, catching three scope gaps per bid is worth more than it was two years ago.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How do rising material costs increase scope gap risk on lump sum bids?


When input prices rise, every unpriced scope item costs more to absorb. A scope gap that was a $200,000 exposure at 2024 material prices may cost significantly more to close at 2026 prices. On a fixed-price contract, that difference comes out of GC margin. The gap between what you priced and what it costs to build widens as material costs rise.


### What is a scope gap in construction?


A scope gap is work that is reasonably part of a project but has no line item in the estimate or subcontract. It may appear in the specifications, be implied by the drawings, or fall in the overlap between two trades. When it surfaces during construction, the GC typically absorbs the cost on a lump sum contract.


### What does "readily inferable" mean in a construction contract?


Readily inferable language requires the contractor to perform work that is reasonably implied by the contract documents, even if it is not explicitly described. On a lump sum contract, this language expands GC responsibility beyond what is written. It is one of the most common sources of scope dispute on commercial projects.


### Which trades carry the most scope gap risk in 2026?


MEP, structural steel, and envelope trades carry elevated risk in 2026 because their input costs are most sensitive to tariff-driven increases. Specialty items like lead-lined glass, generator field conditioning, and roof cover board are also high-risk because they are specification-heavy and commonly missed during document review under time pressure.


### How can a GC protect margin on a lump sum bid when material costs are rising?


The most reliable protection is a tighter scope package before bid day. That means starting from actual drawings and specifications, assigning every trade explicitly, citing specific document references, and running a pre-issue review against the full project document set. Contract risk review before signing also protects against clauses that expand GC liability after award.
